summary: Argues that the Host-IMP interface should run at the highest practical speed. A faster interface reduces delay for short messages queued behind a full-sized one, which could tie up a 100 kbps interface for nearly 100 ms.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 594 argues that faster Host-IMP links can reduce delays and make better use of buffers. BBN's tests measured substantially faster interface operation and higher FTP rates for 36-bit transfers.

questions: why speed up the host to imp link
why did rfc 594 recommend faster host imp interfaces
subtitle: Measurements and reasons for increasing Host-IMP interface speed.

tldr.problem: A 100-kilobaud Host-IMP interface delayed short messages behind large messages, kept buffers occupied and limited communication bandwidth.
tldr.mechanism: BBN tested faster interfaces and measured Host-to-IMP operation at 310 kilobaud and IMP-to-Host operation at 290 kilobaud.
tldr.outcome: The RFC reports higher FTP transfer rates in its experiment and recommends running Host-IMP interfaces at their fastest obtainable speed.

today: RFC 594 is a 1973 report recommending faster Host-IMP interfaces based on BBN experiments.

sections.title: Why Increase Interface Speed
sections.content:
The author argues that the host's interface to its IMP and the IMP's interface to the host should run as fast as possible. At 100 kilobaud, a full-sized message could occupy the interface for almost 100 milliseconds, delaying RFNMs, control messages and NVT characters behind it. Operating at 300 kilobaud would reduce that delay to 30 milliseconds.

Faster transfers would also release host and IMP buffers sooner. The author says higher speed could make it practical to wait for all packets of a multi-packet message to reach the destination host before returning an RFNM, reducing a source of undetected errors.
sections.plainLanguage: A large message on a slow interface can delay smaller messages and control signals. Faster transfers also free buffers sooner and could make stronger error handling practical.

sections.title: Measured Interface and FTP Rates
sections.content:
In BBN's experiment, the Host-to-IMP connection used a two-way handshake and reached a burst bandwidth of 310 kilobaud. The IMP-to-Host connection used a four-way handshake and reached 290 kilobaud. Both systems were operating at the higher interface speed.

For one-megabit FTP file transfers, the table reports 36-bit Image rates of 79 kilobaud for Get and 85 kilobaud for Send. The report contrasts this with a typical pre-speedup 36-bit rate of 25 kilobaud and gives CPU use separately for each operation.
sections.plainLanguage: The tests measured 310 kilobaud from host to IMP and 290 kilobaud in the other direction. FTP tests also showed 36-bit Image transfer rates around 80 kilobaud in this setup.

sections.title: Recommendation
sections.content: The report recommends that all Host-IMP interfaces in the network be sped up to the fastest operation obtainable. It notes that local host interfaces shorter than 30 feet might run faster than 300 kilobaud, based on the propagation delay measured for the distant host driver-receiver pair.
sections.plainLanguage: The author recommends using each Host-IMP interface at its fastest obtainable speed. The report says shorter local interfaces might support even higher speeds.
